quarterly_data.signal: THE CAPITAL RAISE IS A SUBSTRATE-AND-FAB SPENDING EVENT: Zinsner explained the August equity raise as 'the capital raise precedes capital investment' - 2026 CapEx has already been upticked 'by a couple of billion dollars from $18 billion to $20 billion', next year's will be significantly higher, and 'substrates are really constrained and we're going to need to make investments associated with substrates as well next year, given the significant demand.' Committing to 14A high-volume manufacturing in 2028 means placing long-lead supplier orders now, which was one of the biggest drivers of the raise. On footprint: Ireland's shell is being equipped now; Fab 52 in Arizona is running Intel 18A and Fab 62 is almost ready, with next year's investment accelerating its equipping; Oregon stays the pilot line but will also run volume Intel 14A as 18A is pushed into Arizona; Ohio shells are in progress with the ability to have 'eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio', mod one being built as fast as possible. Zinsner said 2027 CapEx is not locked - the businesses gave him a number and 'I've told them no', sending them back for more efficiency before he guides.
quarterly_data.figure: from $18 billion to $20 billion; eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio

quarterly_data.signal: INTEL 14A: 0.9 PDK IN OCTOBER, RISK PRODUCTION 2027, HIGH-VOLUME 2028: Zinsner said Intel is within two months of the 14A 0.9 PDK, so 'you can pretty much now expect us to land in October with that 0.9 PDK', and the remaining step from 0.9 to 1.0 is much smaller than 0.5 to 0.9. Defect density on Intel 14A is tracking better than the target curve and is coming down faster than any previous node - 'we haven't seen this performance since 22 nanometer, which is arguably one of the best nodes Intel's ever put out' - while 18A yields are beating internal milestones. Demand side: internal product teams, 'probably the most cynical bunch out of anybody', are now designing products on Intel 14A, and external foundry engagements have increased enough that Lip-Bu Tan and the team meet customers weekly and the conversation has moved from data to 'how much capacity can I get? What does that supply look like?'. That sequence forces risk production in 2027 ahead of high-volume manufacturing in 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: 0.9 PDK in October; risk production in 2027; high volume production in 2028; 22 nanometer

quarterly_data.signal: EMIB-T ADVANCED PACKAGING SIZED FOR THE FIRST TIME - REVENUE FROM 2H 2027, MULTIPLE BILLIONS PER CUSTOMER: Zinsner said EMIB-T, which removes the interposer from EMIB and can increase reticle size significantly, is a differentiated solution not available elsewhere, and that packaging revenue will 'start to ramp in the back half of 2027', become a run-rate business in 2028 and be 'definitely hitting its stride in 2029'. Scale: 'this business is in the billions... by customer, it will be multiple billion dollars per customer per year of business', at margins of '40% gross, 30% operating margin' with low capital intensity relative to the front end, so 'the ROIC is phenomenal'. He framed advanced packaging as the on-ramp that tests Intel operationally and creates cross-sell into front-end foundry, something Intel has 'already seen that show up even now'. He also pointed to the hire of Seokhee, former CEO of SK hynix, to lead the business as the signal of the opportunity size.
quarterly_data.figure: back half of 2027; multiple billion dollars per customer per year; 40% gross, 30% operating margin

quarterly_data.signal: INTEL 3 OFFERED AS A BASE-DIE PROCESS FOR OTHER COMPANIES: Asked whether the Ireland Intel 3/4 nodes are internal-only, CFO David Zinsner said 'Intel 3 would not be a great logic process for external, but we use it for base die, and it can be used for base die for other companies. And the fact that we have advanced packaging and all these things kind of all under one roof, there could potentially be some opportunities there.'
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: COMPONENT SQUEEZE - DRAM, NAND AND SUBSTRATES: CFO Zinsner said 'over the last several months, industry-wide supply for key components like DRAM, NAND and substrates has come under increasing pressure due to intense demand to support the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure', and rising component pricing, especially relative to the client market, 'could limit our revenue opportunity this year'. CEO Tan called the memory constraint and pricing 'a very big challenge' for the industry: bigger OEM and hyperscale players have more access to memory while smaller ones 'are really challenging to scramble to get the memory', so Intel is allocating CPUs to customers that can complete products ('We don't want to have a CPU, we sent to them, but they are missing the memory'). CFO Zinsner added that for Lunar Lake, Intel was 'relatively aggressive in terms of getting the memory early', though those margins are low because the memory is in package.

quarterly_data.signal: 1.6T optical-module PCB: current orders are mainly 1.6T high-speed optical-module boards; 2026 optical-module related revenue is guided to double, 1.6T keeps growing sharply in 2027 and becomes the main shipping spec in 2028, and 3.2T boards are already being sampled. Customers are already pre-booking 2027 capacity; target is to become the world's largest high-end optical-module PCB supplier in 2027. 800G-and-above optical-module boards require M7-class ultra-low-loss laminate (1.6T effectively mandates it); management says roughly 20 players claim to be entering optical modules but few master M7 high-layer board production, which is why Zhen Ding's substrate-derived M7 technology gave it the 1.6T breakout. 1.6T optical-module board yield is described as industry-leading at above 90%, including the newly ramped Thailand lines. On a potential US FCC ban on Chinese optical modules: Zhen Ding supplies the PCB inside the module, not the module itself, so sees no direct hit, and can shift production to Thailand where customers require it. On CPO: the company says it will participate in both pluggable and CPO/NPO architectures as they develop; most PCB equipment is transferable between product types so a CPO shift would strand little capacity.

Thailand: PA01 reached breakeven and turned profitable in July 2026 (mass production began Q3 2025); additional Thai buildings and a data/computing center complete around end-2026; Thai plants 1-2 make server and optical-module boards, plant 3 flex, plant 4 high-layer-count server boards. Shenzhen third campus broke ground 07-24-2026 for AI 1.6T optical-module high-layer boards and high-end AI flex; its supplier conference drew 217 supply-chain companies and 410 representatives. Capacity for the next three years is largely bound to customers through LTAs and project-based binding agreements (visibility to 2029); 2027 AI PCB order visibility described as optimistic with capacity still insufficient. By 2030 the target is server + optical-module + IC-substrate at 45% to 50% of group revenue. GPU customer motherboards are produced both in mainland China and Thailand depending on customer requirements. Subsidiary Peng Ding filed its Hong Kong main-board listing application on July 2, 2026 (under review, so details withheld).

contracts.signal: A 10-YEAR ADVANCED PACKAGING AGREEMENT between TSMC and Amkor: 'the agreement establishes a framework to expand advanced packaging and test capacity while strengthening the U.S. semiconductor supply chain'. By combining TSMC's leading-edge wafer fabrication with Amkor's advanced packaging and test expertise the two aim to give customers 'more integrated manufacturing solutions, spanning advanced silicon fabrication through advanced packaging and test' and to build 'a more resilient semiconductor ecosystem in ARIZONA', enabling faster time to market.

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging capacity is 'VERY TIGHT also' — TSMC is working with OSAT partners to increase capacity on top of its own expansion. Supplies the LARGEST reticle-size packaging today (large CoWoS); CoPoS pilot line is built NOW with production expected 'a couple of years later'; SoIC and system-on-wafer also in the toolkit. Key engineering challenges at giant die sizes: mechanical stress, warpage and thermal limitation — 'the harder the better'. Note: customers exploring competitor EMIB for larger reticle sizes; TSMC says it leaves no business on the table.
quarterly_data.figure: Adv packaging very tight; CoPoS pilot now -> production ~2028

quarterly_data.signal: PACKAGING IS NOW THE BINDING CONSTRAINT — CEO C.C. Wei, asked about competitors' EMIB-T gaining traction: 'our PACKAGING CAPACITY IS SO TIGHT that now it's LIMITING MY CUSTOMERS' GROWTH. We welcome that additional flexibility in the market. That will help TSMC's front-end wafer business growth, which is a majority part of TSMC's business... We hope they will be successful, that share some of the loading from TSMC. Today, we're working very hard to shorten the gap between the demand and the capacity.' TSMC is explicitly willing to let a rival packaging technology absorb overflow because front-end wafer is the larger profit pool. Capacity response: the newly announced ADDITIONAL $100 BILLION ARIZONA INVESTMENT includes ADVANCED PACKAGING FABS alongside 2nm-and-below logic fabs, and 13 leading-edge and advanced-packaging fabs are being built in Taiwan over the next several years; 10-20% of the raised $60-64B 2026 capital budget goes to advanced packaging, testing and mask making.
quarterly_data.figure: 'Packaging capacity so tight it's LIMITING customers' growth'; +$100B Arizona incl. adv packaging fabs

quarterly_data.signal: GLASS SUBSTRATE / NEXT-GEN PACKAGING STATUS: asked about progress on glass core, glass substrate and glass carrier alongside the roadmap to beyond-14x-reticle CoWoS, C.C. Wei said 'today, the MAJORITY IS STILL CoWoS... We are developing that alternative, try to LOWER DOWN THE COST. We also work with a SUBSTRATE VENDOR so that our customer can have their product be in the market.' On timing: the previously announced PILOT LINE is being built and 'it will take about ANOTHER ONE YEAR TO BE MATURE so we can put it into the production with our customer' — i.e. glass-based production insertion around mid-2027 at the earliest.
quarterly_data.figure: Glass substrate pilot line ~1 more year to maturity before customer production; CoWoS still the majority

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging sizing (CFO): revenue contribution from advanced packaging in 2025 was 'close to 10%. quarterly_data.signal: High-bandwidth flash (HBF): asked whether HBF is a TCB or vertical-wire opportunity, Lester Wong said "it is a TCB play, not for vertical wire" (probably the APTURA tool). HBF is designed to merge NAND-level capacity with HBM-class performance and targets to match HBM bandwidth with 8 to 16x capacity; it is still in early stages, multiple packaging technologies may be used, and K&S is exploring it with a few customers. The next milestone would probably be shipping a system before a PO, and commercial timing is "probably be more of a CY '27 play."
quarterly_data.figure: HBF targets 8 to 16x capacity at HBM bandwidth; expected to be more of a CY '27 play

quarterly_data.signal: Vertical wire (K&S says it pioneered the technology) is its other DRAM opportunity, a cost-effective die-stacking alternative for bandwidth; customer feedback is positive and management anticipates strong sequential growth in both TCB and vertical wire over the coming years. It is gaining traction with some volume possibly in the latter half of FY '26 but expanding much more in FY '27; "We're currently working with 8 customers in Korea, China and the U.S. on this." Together with the HBM system shipped to the leading memory maker, this is K&S's move from its traditionally NAND-heavy memory business into DRAM.

TSMC is looking at how to release more capacity' given fab constraints - taking its lower-end process steps and outsourcing those to the OSATs to free precious fab capacity for the higher end. Plisinski said that dynamic was in play in the order, and that OSAT capital intensity is really volume-driven, with the volume expected to come both from that outsourced capacity and from the OSATs' own technology that they will be selling. On share at the OSATs versus the foundries, Onto has very high share on the 2D side at the higher-end applications and has gained nice traction on 3D bump metrology at at least a couple of the OSATs; share is lower in low-end or China work.

Within advanced packaging the memory (HBM) versus 2.5D logic mix is fairly well split, generally around the 50/50 mark or 60/40 depending on the quarter, because logic requires the memory around it so the whole packaging requirement grows across both. On share, Onto has always had very high share in memory and maintained it, with incremental gains tied to 3D bump metrology as bumps get smaller and denser (3DI); in logic packaging there is room to gain share because of the very high resolution the Dragonfly G5 provides.

quarterly_data.quarter: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: First sizing of the panel-level packaging opportunity: Plisinski said Onto has publicly put the market at around a $1 billion SAM (competitors have said even more), covering process control - inspection as well as lithography - and that while Onto will not get 100% of it against competitors, '$200 million, $300 million' would be a reasonable expectation over the next few years. The accelerant is that constraints in AI packaging and heterogeneous integration are pushing customers to panel as an alternative: as die and therefore packages get bigger the economies of scale at the wafer level stop working - at 310 by 310 they get better, but that is still much smaller than 600 by 600 or 510 by 515 - so customers are moving capacity to companies with a proven process that can ramp right now. Adoption is still early and management expects it to continue over the next several years. The enterprise-server driver (advanced IC substrates, where Intel and AMD were constrained during COVID) is also working its way back, addressed by the JetStep X500 and Firefly.
quarterly_data.figure: around a $1 billion SAM; Onto share expectation $200 million, $300 million over the next few years

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging grew over 25% sequentially in Q4, driven by Dragonfly inspection, Iris films metrology and established 2.5D applications; sales from the 2.5D packaging business doubled versus Q3. Advanced packaging and specialty devices were approximately $145 million in Q4 (slightly more than half of revenue, including approximately $9 million from Semilab) and $504 million for 2025. 2026 outlook: advanced packaging revenue to grow over 30%, a new record ('It's OSATs, it's panel. It's all of advanced packaging.'), and 'relatively stable' between the first half and second half; the guide assumes no large Dragonfly G5 adoption ('We've taken a conservative approach there'), so G5 could add second-half upside. CEO: 'the vast majority of that 30% growth is all tied to supporting the strong demand in AI'; Onto no longer splits out AI packaging because many OSATs and specialty packaging customers are joining that supply chain. CoWoS and HBM inspection growth in 2026 is expected to be relatively similar (CoWoS has higher capital intensity); G5 wins could swing it toward CoWoS.
quarterly_data.figure: advanced packaging and specialty devices approximately $145 million in Q4, $504 million for 2025; advanced packaging to grow over 30% in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Next-generation inspection: Onto is supporting 4 separate customer evaluations of its next-generation inspection systems (the G5, which the analyst described as Onto's 'new high-resolution Dragonfly platform') at customers' facilities. Preliminary feedback is positive, citing significant improvement in optical performance and higher throughput. The qualifications target 2.5D packaging and high-bandwidth memory, including next-generation hybrid bonding, where current-generation tools are already used for process control and R&D. The timeline is unchanged: 'accelerated evaluations to end in the Q1, Q2, the first half of the year with hopefully starting to catch ramps in the second half of the year.' 3D metrology is becoming more crucial for die stacking and fan-out, and the 3Di metrology pipeline is expanding beyond HBM. Semilab's surface charge metrology, which addresses residual charge on die in large-format heterogeneous packaging, received its first orders.
quarterly_data.figure: 4 separate customer evaluations of next-generation inspection systems; evaluations to end in the first half of the year

quarterly_data.signal: Panel-level packaging: Onto won orders in the quarter for JetStep and 8 Firefly systems to support 'an exciting new large panel packaging facility'. The orders are 'the first of several potential phases of expansion', and the panel customer serves AI applications. Multiple advanced-packaging customers placed further 3Di purchase orders, including an OEM that needs precise metrology for new panel-level process development. Customers are adopting Firefly process control in glass and panel fan-out, feeding metrology into the stepper for shot-by-shot adjustments, and JetStep prints large packages without stitching. In lithography, after a period of heavy industry overcapacity, customers are 'beginning to resume orders'. Onto expects this to increase into 2027, and the data suggests 2027 'will be in supply-demand where there's just not enough supply to meet the demand'. CEO: end customers such as 'the AMDs, et cetera, are looking for alternatives' to traditional advanced packaging so they can scale.
quarterly_data.figure: orders for JetStep and 8 Firefly systems for a new large panel packaging facility

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and supply: Onto is set up to serve a $2 billion run rate, and that has 'only improved as we bring up the extended factories', with a transition period over the next couple of quarters while those factories ramp. On constraints: 'I don't see capacity being a big issue for us. It's more on the supply chain side'. Fast order growth and customer pull-ins are straining suppliers, 'especially in the area of precision optics', where lead times are relatively fixed, and Onto is working with customers and suppliers to manage 'tightening capacity and the gradual extension of lead times'. Backlog nearly doubled over the last 3 months to a record of approximately 2 quarters, and several customers' forecasts now extend into 2027. More than 50% of tools were delivered from the extended factories in Q4.

quarterly_data.signal: Mix and pricing: a broad laminate price-increase wave hit in Q2 - the lower the grade, the larger the hike (specific increases not disclosed, they vary by customer). Despite low-end prices rising more, mix still shifted up: M7/M8 ultra-low-loss laminates rose from 38% to 39% of revenue while mid/low-loss M4/M6 grades slipped from 32% to 31%, so the product mix keeps optimising toward the high end and management sees plenty of margin headroom left. The special-products line (thick-copper and special-resin boards supporting power applications) nearly doubled its share over four quarters - 8% in Q3 2025, 10% in Q4 2025, 12% in Q1 2026, 14% in Q2 - with management calling TUC a leader in that niche.

quarterly_data.signal: Kuprion (CEO): the company made product qualification milestone payments in Q1 2026 and is in the final innings before ramping capacity at its first significant site in California; the pipeline of demand already exceeds the first site's production capacity, so a second site is being planned; the first plant should be ramped to full production in the second half of 2026, with guidance of multiple millions of dollars of revenue in '26 and a material EBITDA contribution in '27. Kuprion is not yet used in high-volume manufacturing anywhere; one application is Through-Glass Vias, the core layers for some of the highest-end printed circuit boards, where it solves a major customer pain point. 2025 capex advanced Kuprion and new advanced packaging product manufacturing.
quarterly_data.figure: multiple millions of dollars of revenue in '26; material EBITDA contribution in '27

quarterly_data.signal: New products and outgrowth (CEO): traction in power electronics, Kuprion, die attach solutions, circuit board fabrication and thermal materials drives part of the outgrowth versus the market, and the technology skews to the highest-end applications, such as the highest value circuit boards growing well in excess of the market. Argomax is broadening its customer base, with 20-plus percent growth in the back half of 2025 outside the original core customer, expected to continue; the power electronics business is "gaining share in excess of the automotive market".
quarterly_data.figure: Argomax 20-plus percent growth outside the original core customer in the back half of 2025

quarterly_data.signal: Market color (CEO): memory prices are rising because capacity is constrained by surging data center demand; this could hurt consumer electronics, but Element has more value on a high-end data center server board than in a PC or smartphone, and its 2026 forecast assumes quite strong data center growth but no strong smartphone or consumer electronics growth. The PCB baseline is Prismark: a 6% year in 2026 and a 9% CAGR from '24 to '29. Element is driven by board volume, not board dollar value, and growth is concentrated in high-value complex boards. For the past 3 years PCB square-meter growth has exceeded MSI growth; in 2025 PCB square meters grew high single digits versus Circuitry at 10%, and MSI grew mid-single digits versus Semi in the low teens, with similar outperformance expected in 2026. Activity in Asia in early January was described as unbelievable.
quarterly_data.figure: Prismark PCB baseline 6% in 2026; 9% CAGR from '24 to '29

quarterly_data.signal: Portfolio (CFO/CEO): both acquisitions closed early in Q1 2026 for approximately $870 million, funded in part by a new $450 million term loan add-on; pro forma leverage is slightly above 3x and expected to approach 2.5x by year-end 2026. Micromax (advanced electronics inks and pastes plus low-temperature ceramic materials for satellites, EVs and data centers) had roughly $40 million of 2025 EBITDA and organic revenue growth north of 10%. EFC Gases & Advanced Materials (high-purity specialty gases and advanced materials, concentrated in semiconductor fabrication, electrical infrastructure and satellite propulsion, with a revenue CAGR above 15% since 2009 and recent growth mainly in semiconductor applications) had roughly $30 million and sits in the Specialty segment. Both are outperforming initial expectations. The slower-growth Graphics (flexographic printing) business was divested in Q1 2025.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately $870 million paid; Micromax roughly $40 million EBITDA in '25; EFC roughly $30 million
